analysis.one_liner: Bans deceptive unsolicited bulk email and lets email recipients and providers sue spammers.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Gene Green with 9 bipartisan cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing in late 1999 and died in committee without ever reaching a House or Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The E-Mail User Protection Act would have made it illegal to send unsolicited bulk commercial email with fake sender names, return addresses, or header information, and to keep emailing people after they asked to be left alone. It would also have banned selling software built to forge email identities, let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules, and let email users and internet providers sue violators for $50 per message or $10,000 per day plus attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday email users, who would gain a legal right to stop spam they had opted out of and to sue senders that forged their identities. Internet and email providers would also gain, since they could sue senders whose forged messages clog their networks, recovering damages and attorney fees.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to send unsolicited bulk email carrying a false, fictitious, or misappropriated sender name or return address, or with knowledge that the message forges an Internet domain, header, timestamp, or originating address.
Requires bulk email senders to honor a recipient's request to stop receiving messages, and makes ignoring that request unlawful.
Bans using, creating, selling, or distributing software primarily designed to forge email identities and headers, cutting off the tooling behind the abuse.

Lets the Federal Trade Commission enforce violations as an unfair or deceptive practice, and gives both recipients and interactive computer services a private right to sue for $50 per message or $10,000 per day, plus injunctions and attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Bulk email senders and the direct email marketing industry, which would face civil fines of up to $50 per message or $10,000 per day, criminal penalties for deliberate identity theft or ignoring opt-outs, FTC enforcement, and lawsuits from recipients and internet providers. Sellers of email-forgery software would lose their market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bulk email marketers and forgery-software sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill targets deception and opt-out violations, not unsolicited email itself: a marketer could still send any volume of commercial email as long as the sender information was accurate and opt-out requests were honored, so inboxes would not have gone spam-free.

The per-message penalty of $50 available to any adversely affected recipient, with attorney fees attached, could have invited high-volume litigation that punishes technical violations as much as genuine fraud.
Enforcement would be hard in practice: senders who deliberately forge headers are difficult to identify and pursue, so the FTC and private suits might reach only a fraction of violators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: this was a first-generation anti-spam bill aimed at the most abusive conduct, forged identities and ignored opt-outs, not at bulk email generally. The costs fall on a marketing industry that was profiting from deceptive mail, though the litigation-friendly penalties and the narrow scope mean the bill would likely have restrained the worst actors more than it cleaned up inboxes.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House committees for a year and a half, got a single subcommittee hearing, and died when the Congress ended without any committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green of Texas introduced the bill on May 24, 1999, and it was sent to both the Commerce and Judiciary Committees.
In June 1999 it went to the Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee, and in September 1999 also to the Crime Subcommittee, splitting it across two panels.
The subcommittees held a hearing on November 3, 1999, but neither committee ever voted to report the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bulk email marketers came out ahead: without a law on the books, they could keep sending unsolicited commercial mail with no federal penalties for forged sender information or ignored opt-out requests, and email users kept absorbing the cost in clutter and fraud.

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support: 8 Democrats and 1 Republican.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (Chair Tom Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee, which held one hearing in November 1999 and never reported the bill out of committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Second committee of jurisdiction (Chair Henry Hyde)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime Subcommittee in September 1999 and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan (8 Democrats and 1 Republican among the 9 cosponsors), but no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.industry: Bulk email marketers and direct email advertising
industries.note: The bill's fines ($50 per message or $10,000 per day), criminal penalties, FTC enforcement, and private lawsuits fall squarely on senders of unsolicited commercial email, whose business model depends on mailing large volumes at near-zero cost. Its interest runs against email users, who bear the spam.

industries.industry: Sellers of email-forgery and address-harvesting software
industries.note: The bill bans creating, selling, or distributing software primarily designed to forge email identities and headers, eliminating this niche market outright.

Providers get a private right to sue senders whose forged messages transit their networks, recovering damages, injunctions, and attorney fees; cleaning spam also cuts their bandwidth and abuse-handling costs.
